issues.legal_issue: An unregistered compromise instrument intended to create a long-term lease does not itself create an interest in the immovable property, although it may be used for limited purposes.
material_facts: A prior ejectment decree had been passed against the occupant.
A later compromise provided for a sixteen-year lease, but neither a lease deed nor a registration of the compromise was made.
The occupant's possession after the decree was based on the compromise.
issues.conclusion: The compromise required registration to create the leasehold interest; because it was unregistered, it did not affect the property or create an interest in it. It remained admissible as evidence of part performance for the purpose of section 53A of the Transfer of Property Act or of a collateral transaction not requiring a registered instrument.
issues.legal_principle: An instrument intended to create a lease affecting immovable property must be registered to affect that property. The unregistered compromise could not be received as evidence of a transaction affecting the property, subject to its admissibility for section 53A of the Transfer of Property Act or a collateral transaction. The Court also applied the distinction between the limited statutory protection under section 53A and the creation of an interest in property.

predicates.possession_recovery_suit: A party brings a proceeding to recover possession of immovable property.
predicates.unregistered_compromise_purports_to_crea: The parties use an unregistered compromise instrument to provide for a long-term lease of immovable property.

issues.definition: When a possession-recovery proceeding concerns an unregistered compromise purporting to create a long-term lease, the compromise creates no leasehold interest in the property.

issues.legal_issue: Part performance under section 53A of the Transfer of Property Act gives a transferee in possession a defensive right, not an active title to the property.
material_facts: The occupant entered or continued in possession on the basis of an unregistered compromise providing for a lease.
The occupant paid the monthly amount required by the compromise during the intended lease term.
issues.conclusion: The occupant's performance of the contract brought the occupant within section 53A, but that section gave only a right to defend possession and conferred no active title or interest in the property.
issues.legal_principle: Section 53A of the Transfer of Property Act provides a statutory bar against the transferor, available as a defence to a transferee who has performed or is willing to perform the contract; it does not confer active title. The Court relied on Sheth Maneklal Mansukhbhai v. M/s. Hormusji Jamshedii Ginwalla and Sons, which described section 53A as a partial importation of the English doctrine of part performance, and Probodh Kumar Das v. Dantmara Tea Company Ltd., concerning the absence of active title under section 53A.

predicates.part_performance_defense_claim: A person relies on part performance as a defence to a claim affecting that person's possession.
predicates.transferee_in_possession_under_void_tran: A transferee is in possession under a transfer that is ineffective to create an interest in the property.
predicates.transferee_performed_or_willing_to_perfo: The transferee performed, or is willing to perform, the transferee's obligations under the contract.

issues.definition: If a person in possession under an ineffective transfer relies on part performance as a defence and has performed or is willing to perform the contract, the protection is defensive and does not confer title.

issues.legal_issue: Payment and acceptance of amounts described as rent under an ineffective lease do not, by themselves, establish a tenancy; the parties' intention must be determined from the facts and circumstances.
material_facts: A prior ejectment decree had been passed, and the later compromise provided for a sixteen-year lease at a monthly rent.
The occupant paid the stipulated monthly amount during the intended lease term, and the owners accepted the payments and issued receipts.
The courts found that the payments were made in performance of the compromise, not independently of it, and no payment after the stated lease term was claimed.
The occupant claimed that the payments and their acceptance created a monthly tenancy protected by the West Bengal Premises Tenancy Act, 1956.
issues.conclusion: The payments and their acceptance did not create a tenancy on the facts found, because they were made in part performance of the compromise. The tenancy claim therefore failed.
issues.legal_principle: Whether a landlord-tenant relationship exists depends on whether the parties intended to create a tenancy, an intention to be inferred from the facts and circumstances. Payments made under the contract and accepted as rent do not alone establish a tenancy; payments independent of the contract may, depending on the facts, support such an inference. The Court distinguished Ram Kumar Das v. Jagadish Chandra Deb, which did not establish that every payment under an invalid lease creates a monthly tenancy, and referred to State of Punjab v. British India Corporation Ltd. on the meaning of rent. It also applied section 53A of the Transfer of Property Act in treating the payments as performance of the contract rather than as proof of a tenancy.

rule.if: tenancy_claim_after_void_lease and payments_required_by_contract and landlord_accepted_payments and payments_not_independent_of_contract

predicates.tenancy_claim_after_void_lease: A person in possession under an ineffective lease claims that a tenancy exists.
predicates.payments_required_by_contract: The payments relied on to establish tenancy were required by the contract underlying the ineffective lease.
predicates.landlord_accepted_payments: The owner accepted the payments made by the occupant.
predicates.payments_not_independent_of_contract: The payments were made as performance of the contract rather than independently of it.

issues.definition: When a tenancy is claimed after an ineffective lease, payments required by the contract and accepted by the owner do not alone establish tenancy if those payments were not independent of the contract.
